**Playbook for ref_commons**

1. On the opening season, I take roughly the stated sustainable share, maybe just under, to establish a cooperative tone and keep the stock at full regrowth.

2. While all boats land at or below the sustainable share and the stock holds steady, I keep submitting the sustainable share exactly. Cooperation held up perfectly in the last run — the stock stayed at 100 all game.

3. If rivals land slightly below the sustainable share, I do not match them; I stick to my stated share. A rival consistently landing 10 instead of 11.1 cost me nothing and matching them would only have reduced my total.

4. I watch the stock after each season. If the stock stays near the cap, the sustainable-share figure stays reliable and I keep using it. If the stock starts falling meaningfully, I cut back toward (or below) the new lower sustainable share rather than chasing rivals.

5. On the final season, there is no future to protect: I take a larger catch while the stock is healthy. Taking 22 when the sustainable share was 11.1 worked cleanly and the fishery was in no danger. Roughly doubling is safe with a full stock — this is free payoff. I could test being slightly greedier here (e.g. 25–30 of a 100 stock), since collapse only matters if it hits zero and there are no further seasons to protect.

6. Never take so much in any season that the stock risks collapsing — total catch across all boats approaching the remaining stock is the real danger, and my marginal greed should never be the cause of it.

7. Don't overfish early: small early gains cost future sustainable yield and invite rivals to defect too. Steady near-sustainable play plus one endgame grab produced a high, stable total — that's the shape of the optimal strategy.

8. Don't overthink the middle seasons. Once cooperation is established and the stock is holding at cap, the correct move is mechanical: submit the sustainable share every time and save the reasoning for the final round.

9. Cooperation can emerge and persist even with no communication. One rival started below quota (10 vs 11.1) and then converged to the sustainable share by season 3 — restraint early appears to signal trustworthiness, so keep the opening seasons conservative.

10. If a season ever comes where the number of remaining seasons is small but not final, the same endgame logic applies with a discount: grab only what still leaves enough stock to regrow for the remaining seasons. Full greed is reserved strictly for the last round.

**Playbook — ref_commons**

- On the first season I submit exactly the sustainable share. Opening below it (I once did 10 when the share was 11.1) costs a full fish for no strategic benefit.

- I track the leader's cumulative total from the season reports. My goal is to stay level with or above the top rival. A small persistent deficit is tolerable, but I should not drift behind — and if rivals consistently under-fish the sustainable share, that is free fish for me: I still take the full share while they fall behind.

- When rivals cooperate at the sustainable share, staying exactly at that share is enough — confirmed again: five seasons at 11.1 kept the stock pinned at 100 and my total above both rivals. No need for mid-game overages when I am level or ahead.

- Mid-game (two or more seasons remaining after the current one), I submit at or just above the sustainable share — no more than ~1 unit above. Larger grabs shrink the stock and cut everyone's sustainable share for remaining seasons, costing me more than the grab gained.

- On the penultimate season, I compute the final-season stock effect of any overage before choosing it; a small overage is fine only if next season's sustainable share barely drops. If rivals are steady cooperators, as here, staying at the share through season 5 was correct.

- On the final season, there is no future to protect, so I take much more than the sustainable share. My rule: estimate what the rivals will take (recent seasons are a good guide — here they took 11.1 each), then grab roughly the remaining stock minus their expected total, with a safety margin of ~15-20 units. I took 33 of 100 when I could safely have taken closer to 60-70; the rivals' totals do not expand to fill the gap. Conservative third-of-stock is a floor, not a target.

- Before submitting any final-season grab, I sanity-check that the sum of all boats' catches stays comfortably under the stock — collapse to zero ends all scoring. Same check applies any season total requests approach the stock.

- General rule: match the sustainable share while the horizon is long, stay competitive with rivals mid-game, and exploit hard in the endgame — sized to what the stock can actually absorb, not just a rough fraction.

# Playbook for the shared fishery game

**Baseline rule:** When cooperation is holding, submit exactly the stated sustainable share (rounded down slightly if I want to signal restraint). This kept the stock at 100 for all six seasons and maximized total landings. Never drift above sustainable mid-game.

**Early restraint pays:** Taking 10 while the stated share was 11.1 for two seasons cost almost nothing and may have nudged rivals toward stable full-cooperation behavior. Cheap goodwill; do it early. Note: rivals never reciprocated the restraint — they took the full 11.1 — so don't keep sacrificing share season after season. One or two seasons of signaling is enough; then match the stated share.

**Match rivals, don't escalate:** If others land slightly above or below sustainable, match their level. Cooperation here was remarkably stable across two playthroughs — no one defected early, and the stock never declined. Don't defect preemptively mid-game on a fear that never materialized.

**Last season: defect hard, and don't be shy about size.** Two episodes confirm the rule. With stock at 100 and no future value, taking 2x sustainable scored +75.2; taking 30 (~2.7x sustainable) scored +83.3. The larger defection worked with no downside — the game ends after the catch, so post-catch stock collapse doesn't matter. Next time, consider going much higher (50+, even most of the stock): the only cap is what the harbour actually lets me land, and rivals defecting too costs me nothing since there's no tomorrow.

**Key principle:** In finite-horizon commons games, cooperate at (or just under) the sustainable share every season except the last, then defect big. The cooperation phase worked perfectly twice — the only real decision is the size of the final defection, and bigger has been better both times. Push the final number up until something penalizes it.

**Watch the numbers, not the narrative:** Each season the display showed the stock holding exactly at 100. As long as that pattern holds, keep cooperating. Only adjust if the stock actually starts declining or rivals visibly overfish.

**Season counting discipline:** In season 6/6 I initially planned to defect in the final season and executed it. Keep a clear count of remaining seasons — the value of defecting rises sharply as the horizon approaches, and the end-of-game defection is where most of my edge over naive cooperators comes from.
